section_name: Step 1 Introduce — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Informative writing. Step 1 — Introduce.

Teacher script: "Writers, we have been learning how to collect important facts from a text before writing a report. Today, I am going to teach you how to continue researching the same topic USING A SECOND SOURCE. As we read another text, we will collect additional, smaller details and KEEP TRACK of which facts come from which source."

This introduction is used across all grade levels K-5 on Day 3.

section_name: Step 2A Tell — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (K-2)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grades K-2. Step 2A — Tell the Children (5 minutes).

Teacher script: "We have been learning how to research a topic before we write a report. We've learned how to jot down the big facts about the topic—the who, what, where, when, why, and how.

Today we are going to continue researching the same topic using a second source. Say 'source.' A source is a place to get information about a topic. A source can be a book, an article, a website, etc. One source can't tell us everything. A second source may teach us something new. It adds smaller details to help us understand the big ideas even better. So today, we will read a second source and collect new, little details.

WHY the skill is important: Including smaller details in your report does two important things: 1) It helps your reader learn more, and 2) It makes your writing more interesting. Most writers will include the same big facts—but the little details are what make your report sound different from everyone else's.

WHAT the skill is: Writers don't 'start over' with each new source. They keep their previous research notes. When reading Source 2, you WILL see some of the same big facts again. Writers think to themselves, 'Yep—I already wrote that big fact down.' Writers do not jot down the same facts twice. Instead, look for new, smaller details that were not in the first source. Those are the details to make new research notes about.

HOW the skill works: When we begin Source 2, we need to show that it's a different source. So we switch to a new color of note-taking boxes. That way, we can clearly see which facts came from Source 1 and which came from Source 2. As you read Source 2, pause after a sentence or two and ask yourself: 'Did I learn something new? Did I find a small detail that adds to a big fact I already have?' Little details grow out of big facts—they help explain them and make them clearer.

Identify what new & little details might include:
• A new example (a new type, a new kind, a new way, a new part)
• A describing detail (what it looks like, feels like, sounds like)
• A number detail (how many, how big, how old, when)

Follow the same 4-step process for collecting these new details: 1) READ the text carefully. 2) FIND a fact. 3) SAY the fact in a few words. 4) JOT down the fact phrase.

Each new source helps us add small, interesting details to grow our research notes."

This Step 2A content is used for grades K, 1, and 2 with near-identical wording. The K-2 version uses colored note-taking boxes to distinguish sources.

section_name: Step 2A Tell — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (3-5)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grades 3-5. Step 2A — Tell the Children (5 minutes).

Teacher script: "We've been learning how to research a topic before writing a report. So far, we've collected the big facts (who, what, where, when, why, how) from one author's text.

But when researching, writers always get their information from more than one place. They get information from several sources. A source is any place we get information—a book, article, website. One source cannot tell us everything about a big topic. Different authors provide different details about the same topic.

WHY the skill is important: Including smaller details in your report does two important things: 1) It helps your reader learn more. A report based on only one source is limited. Using multiple sources adds more information and makes the report more complete. 2) It makes your writing more interesting. Most writers include the same big facts—but the little details are what make your report sound different from everyone else's.

WHAT the skill is: Writers don't start their research over with each new source. They keep their previous notes. When reading Source 2, you will see some of the same big facts again. Writers think, 'I already have that.' They do not write the same fact twice. Instead, look for new, smaller details that were not in the first source.

HOW the skill works: When we research from multiple sources, we need to keep the facts organized—what came from which source. So we draw a line at the end of the bulleted facts from Source 1 and start a new section for Source 2.
• Draw a line and add the title & author for each new source.
• Put Source 2 facts on the same paper as Source 1. (If you fill up one note-taking sheet, grab a new sheet and keep going.)
• Write on the front sides only. (Having information on single-sided pages makes it much easier to sort, group, and organize your facts and details later.)

As you read Source 2, pause after a sentence or two and ask, 'Is this new? Does this add to a big fact I already have?' Small details grow from big facts—they explain them and make them clearer. Look for:
• A different example.
• A new vocabulary term (and what it means)
• A description (sensory details, behavior, features).
• A comparison (similar/different, -er/-est, like/as)
• A specific name or type (location, role, person)
• A number detail (measurement/dimensions, date, time, age, temperature, quantity, statistic)

Follow the same 4-step process for collecting these new details: 1) READ the text carefully. 2) FIND a fact. 3) SAY the fact in a few words. 4) JOT down the fact phrase.

Each new source adds small details to your notes—making your research more complete and ultimately your report more specific and interesting."

This Step 2A content is used for grades 3, 4, and 5 with near-identical wording. The 3-5 version uses drawn lines with title & author labels to organize sources on the same paper, rather than colored note-taking boxes.

section_name: Step 2B Show — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade K)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade K. Step 2B — Show the Children (5 minutes). Topic: Space.

Teacher think-aloud script: "Let me show you how I collect research from a second source.

Reveal research notes previously collected from Source 1. Right now I only have 'big facts' about the topic. If I stopped researching now, then my report would sound like everybody else's. I'm going to read a second source on the same topic.

Project Source 2 excerpt (See Source 2, p2, on Space).

First, I need to switch my note paper to a different color. That way I will know that this new information came from Source 2 and not Source 1.

Now I read Source 2 to collect new details using the same 4 steps I used with Source 1.

Step 1: Read. 'Earth is always moving. It rotates, which means it spins in a circle. Earth spins one full time every day.'

Step 2: Find a fact. Hmm... let me think. I already wrote that 'Earth is always moving' and that 'Earth rotates.' (Point to those notes.) But wait... I do NOT have a note that says it spins one full time every day. That is new! That is a little detail about the big fact. I should add a research note.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How can I say that short and clear? 'Spins once a day.' Yes. That's short & clear.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Spins once a day.'

Now I keep reading to see if I can find another new little detail.

Step 1: Read. 'While the Earth spins, it is also traveling around the sun. It takes one whole year for Earth to go all the way around the sun.'

Step 2: Find a fact. Wait a second... the Earth spins... AND it travels around the sun? That is definitely new. I did not write that before.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How could I say that short? 'Takes one whole year around sun.' That's a little long. What about just 'One whole year around sun.' I don't really need 'whole' in front of 'year.' And I can use the numeral 1 instead of writing it out. Yes. That works.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) '1 year around sun.'"

section_name: Step 2B Show — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 1)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 1. Step 2B — Show the Children (5 minutes). Topic: US Symbols.

Teacher think-aloud script: "Let me show you how I collect research from a second source.

Reveal research notes previously collected from Source 1. Right now I only have 'big facts' about the topic. If I stopped researching now, then my report would sound like everybody else's. I'm going to read a second source on the same topic.

Project Source 2 excerpt (See Source 2, p2 on US Symbols).

First, I need to switch my note paper to a different color. That way I will know that this new information came from Source 2 and not Source 1.

Now I read Source 2 to collect new details using the same 4 steps I used with Source 1.

Step 1: Read. 'The American flag can wave on a tall pole. It moves and flutters in the wind. Many schools and buildings fly the flag outside. People stand and show respect when they see the flag.'

Step 2: Find a fact. Hmm... let me think. I already wrote that the flag has 13 stripes. I already wrote that it has 50 stars. (Point to those notes.) But wait... I do NOT have a note that says the flag waves on a tall pole. That is new! That describes how it moves—it waves. That is a little detail about the big fact. I should add a research note.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How can I say that short and clear? 'Waves on tall pole.' Yes. That's pretty simple & still clear.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Waves on tall pole.'

Now I keep reading to see if I can find another new little detail.

Step 1: Read. 'People stand and show respect when they see the flag.'

Step 2: Find a fact. I remember jotting a note about respecting the flag. (Find the note in your previous research.) Right here, I noted that respect meant to 'care for and honor.' But I didn't know that one example of honoring the flag was to stand in front of it. That's a new, little detail.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How could I say that short? 'Respect flag by standing up.' Since standing IS a way to respect, I could use the equal sign instead of 'by.' And I could drop the -ing to make 'standing' a little shorter, too.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Respect flag = stand up.'"

section_name: Step 2B Show — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 2)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 2. Step 2B — Show the Children (5 minutes). Topic: Public Services.

Teacher think-aloud script: "Let me show you how I collect research from a second source.

Reveal research notes previously collected from Source 1. Right now I only have 'big facts' about the topic. If I stopped researching now, then my report would sound like everybody else's.

I don't want to stop researching too soon.

Project Source 2 excerpt (See Source 2, p2 on Public Services).

First, I need to switch my note paper to a different color. That way I will know that this new information came from Source 2 and not Source 1.

Now I read Source 2 to collect new details using the same 4 steps I used with Source 1.

Step 1: Read. 'Communities may have public pools where people can swim. Some pools have lifeguards who watch to keep swimmers safe. There might be a shallow end for younger children and a deep end for stronger swimmers.'

Step 2: Find a fact. Hmm... let me think. I already wrote that communities have public pools for swimming. (Point to that note.) But I do NOT have a note that says anything about a lifeguard to keep swimmers safe. That is new! That is a little detail about the big fact. I need to jot down that new little detail.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How can I say that short and clear? 'Lifeguards keep swimmers safe.' It's a little long still. Since a lifeguard's job IS to keep swimmers safe, I could use the equals sign instead of writing the words.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Lifeguards = swimmers safe.'

Now I keep reading to see if I can find another new little detail.

Step 1: Read. 'There might be a shallow end for younger children and a deep end for stronger swimmers.'

Step 2: Find a fact. That's all new! Including that will add more to my research on public pools as a public service.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How could I say that? 'Shallow and deep ends.' And I could use the 'and' shortcut.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Shallow & deep ends.'"

section_name: Step 2B Show — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 3)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 3. Step 2B — Show the Children (5 minutes). Topic: Simple Machines.

Teacher think-aloud script: "Let me show you how I collect research from a second source.

Reveal research notes previously collected from Source 1. Right now I only have the 'big facts' about the topic. If I stopped researching now, then my report would sound like everybody else's. I don't want to stop researching too soon.

Project Source 2 excerpt (See Source 2, p2 on Simple Machines).

First, I have to draw a line below the bulleted facts of Source 1 and label Source 2 with title and author. This is how I keep my research notes organized so I know which facts came from which source.

Now I will follow the same 4 steps—Read, Find, Say, Jot—and I'll keep checking for NEW information.

Step 1: Read. 'A pulley is another type of simple machine that helps people lift heavy objects. It has a small wheel with a groove around the edge. A rope or cable fits inside that groove so it does not slip off.'

Step 2: Find a fact. I already have that a pulley helps lift heavy objects. (Point to that note.) I also have that it's a wheel with a rope. (Point to that note.) Since I already have that noted, I do not write it twice. But I did NOT have a note about the groove in the wheel. This is a small detail that describes a specific feature of the wheel. It explains how the parts work together.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How can I say that short and clear? 'Groove helps stop it from slipping.' That's a little long. How about: 'Groove stops slipping.' Yes, better.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Groove stops slipping.'

Now I keep reading in small chunks acknowledging big KNOWN facts and recording little NEW details.

Step 1: Read. 'Instead of lifting something straight up with your hands, the pulley helps change the direction of the force.'

Step 2: Find a fact. I already have that a pulley helps lift heavy objects. (Point to that note.) But I do NOT have that it changes the direction of the force. That is new. This is a how-it-works detail. It explains what the pulley actually does to make lifting easier.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How could I say that? 'Pulley changes direction of force.' Since 'pulley' is a main part of this report, I'll abbreviate it to just /P/. 'P changes direction of force.' I could also rearrange the words to make it even shorter: 'P changes force direction.'

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'P changes force direction.'"

section_name: Step 2B Show — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 4)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 4. Step 2B — Show the Children (5 minutes). Topic: Ben Franklin.

Teacher think-aloud script: "Let me show you how I collect research from a second source.

Reveal research notes previously collected from Source 1. Right now I only have the 'big facts' about the topic. If I stopped researching now, then my report would sound like everybody else's. I don't want to stop researching too soon.

Project Source 2 excerpt (See Source 2, p2 on Ben Franklin).

First, I have to draw a line below the bulleted facts of Source 1 and label Source 2 with title and author. This is how I keep my research notes organized so I know which facts came from which source.

Now I will follow the same 4 steps—Read, Find, Say, Jot—looking for NEW information.

Step 1: Read. 'As Benjamin Franklin grew older, he began to have trouble seeing things up close, like books and letters. At the same time, he still needed glasses to see things far away. Instead of switching between two different pairs of glasses, Franklin invented a better solution.'

Step 2: Find a fact. I already have that Franklin invented bifocals. (Point to that note.) I won't write that fact again. But I did NOT know that HE had trouble seeing things up close and far away as he got older, and that HE was using 2 sets of glasses. This explains why he invented bifocals.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How can I say that short and clear? 'Ben Franklin needed 2 pairs of glasses.' Since this is all about Ben Franklin, I'll just abbreviate his name to initials—BF. And I know we say 'pair of glasses' but I'll just write '2 glasses.'

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'BF needed 2 glasses.'

Now I keep reading in small chunks acknowledging big KNOWN facts and recording little NEW details.

Step 1: Read. 'He created bifocals, special glasses that have two viewing areas in one lens. The top half of each lens helps a person see objects that are far away, such as signs or buildings. The bottom half helps with close-up tasks, like reading or sewing.'

Step 2: Find a fact. I already have bifocals improve near & far vision. (Point to that note.) But I do NOT have that the bottom of the lens is for close up and the top is for far away. That's new. It describes how it works.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How could I say that? 'Top is for far away, bottom is for close up.' I could use the equal sign instead of 'is for.' That makes it more efficient.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Top = far away. Bottom = close up.'"

section_name: Step 2B Show — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 5)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 5. Step 2B — Show the Children (5 minutes). Topic: Paul Revere.

Teacher think-aloud script: "Let me show you how I collect research from a second source.

Reveal research notes previously collected from Source 1. Right now I only have the 'big facts' about the topic. If I stopped researching now, then my report would sound like everybody else's. I don't want to stop researching too soon.

Project Source 2 excerpt (See Source 2, p2 on Paul Revere).

First, I have to draw a line below the bulleted facts of Source 1 and label Source 2 with title and author. This is how I keep my research notes organized so I know which facts came from which source.

Now I will follow the same 4 steps—Read, Find, Say, Jot—looking for NEW information.

Step 1: Read. 'Paul Revere was not only a patriot—he was also a skilled silversmith. A silversmith is a person who makes objects out of silver, such as spoons, teapots, cups, and bowls. This work required careful hands and detailed designs, and many people trusted Revere to create important household items.'

Step 2: Find a fact. Now I pause and ask myself: What did I know and did I learn something new? I already noted that Paul Revere was a skilled silversmith. (Point to that note.) But I do NOT have that people trusted him because of his careful, detailed work with important household items. That character detail helps explain why people listened to him.

Step 3: Say it in 1-4 words. How can I say that short and clear? 'Trusted Paul Revere because careful & detailed silversmith with important household items.' WHOA! Way too much! It's about the detail and care he put into his work. If he was that detailed and careful with his work, then he could be trusted with important details and information. So I'll shorten it to: 'Trusted Paul Revere because careful & detailed silversmith.' Better, but still too long. I'll use PR for Paul Revere, since the whole report is about him. And 'bc' for because. And I don't need to say 'silversmith' again.

Step 4: Jot. (Write while talking.) 'Trusted PR bc careful & detailed.'

Now I'd read the next small chunk, acknowledge the big KNOWN facts, and identify any NEW little details."

section_name: Step 3 Interact — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade K)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade K. Step 3 — Interact (5 minutes). Topic: Weather.

Teacher script: "Today we are learning to research a second source & collect new, little details to go with bigger facts we already noted. Help me with the next one."

Source 2 excerpt: "Raindrops can be tiny like dots or big and splashy. When lots of rain falls, it can make puddles on the ground. Rain helps plants and trees grow."

Project a second source on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 2, p4 on Weather. Guide students to switch the color of their note-taking paper to indicate these facts are coming from a new source. Then guide them through the same 4-step process using a series of Turn & Talks: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

New research details:
• rain = tiny or big drops
• rain = helps plants grow

Teacher note: "I will pass out the new colored note-taking handout for you to use."

section_name: Step 3 Interact — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 2)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 2. Step 3 — Interact (5 minutes). Topic: Habitats.

Teacher script: "Today we are learning to research a second source & collect new, little details to go with bigger facts we already noted. Help me with the next one."

Source 2 excerpt: "A rainforest is one of the warmest and wettest habitats on Earth. In fact, many rainforests receive more than 80 inches of rain each year. Because it rains so often, the air feels humid and sticky."

Project a second source on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 2, p4 on Habitats. Guide students to switch the color of their note-taking paper to indicate these facts are coming from a new source. Then guide them through the same 4-step process using a series of Turn & Talks: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

New research details:
• 80+ inches of rain each year
• humid, sticky air

Teacher note: "I will pass out the new colored note-taking handout for you to use."

section_name: Step 3 Interact — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 3)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 3. Step 3 — Interact (5 minutes). Topic: Fossils.

Teacher script: "Today we are learning to research a second source & collect new, little details to go with bigger facts we already noted. Help me with the next one."

Source 2 excerpt: "Paleontologists often work inch by inch and may spend many hours—or even several days—uncovering one fossil. By moving slowly and carefully, they protect the fossil so it can be studied in a lab later."

Project a second source on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 2, p4 on Fossils. Guide students to draw a line to indicate a new source and add the title & author. Then guide them through the same 4-step process using a series of Turn & Talks: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

New research details:
• inch-by-inch digging
• slow & careful → to protect

Teacher note: "Be sure to draw a line below your final research fact from Source 1 before adding research from Source 2."

section_name: Step 3 Interact — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 4)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 4. Step 3 — Interact (5 minutes). Topic: European Exploration.

Teacher script: "Today we are learning to research a second source & collect new, little details to go with bigger facts we already noted. Help me with the next one."

Source 2 excerpt: "Long ago, sailing across the ocean was very difficult and dangerous. Ships were small and not strong enough to travel thousands of miles. Over time, improvements in shipbuilding—the way ships were designed and constructed—made long sea voyages possible."

Project a second source on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 2, p4 on European Exploration. Guide students to draw a line to indicate a new source and add the title & author. Then guide them through the same 4-step process using a series of Turn & Talks: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

New research details:
• early ships = small, weak, dangerous
• new ship designs = stronger

Teacher note: "Be sure to draw a line below your final research fact from Source 1 before adding research from Source 2."

section_name: Step 3 Interact — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details (Grade 5)
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). Grade 5. Step 3 — Interact (5 minutes). Topic: Earth's Spheres.

Teacher script: "Today we are learning to research a second source & collect new, little details to go with bigger facts we already noted. Help me with the next one."

Source 2 excerpt: "Below the crust is the mantle, which is much thicker. In fact, the mantle is about 1,800 miles thick. It is made of hot rock that is mostly solid but can slowly move over time. This slow movement can cause earthquakes and volcanoes."

Project a second source on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about—See Source 2, p4 on Earth's Spheres. Guide students to draw a line to indicate a new source and add the title & author. Then guide them through the same 4-step process using a series of Turn & Talks: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

New research details:
• mantle = 1,800 miles thick
• hot rock moves slowly → quakes/volcanoes

Teacher note: "Be sure to draw a line below your final research fact from Source 1 before adding research from Source 2."

section_name: Step 4 Close — Day 3 Collect Facts & Details
content:
Report Writing Skill #1: Collect facts & details from a text (Day 3 of 3). All grades K-5. Step 4 — Close.

Teacher script: "Today we learned how to collect small details from a second source to add to the big facts we've already researched."

Independent writing task: "During Independent Writing Time you will read a second source on the same topic you have been practicing with. You will use the same four steps to collect new smaller details about big facts you have already noted."

This Step 4 Close is used across all grade levels K-5 with identical wording.
